ECE 6390 / Waves and fields

Helmholtz curvature

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows the connection between a wave’s spatial curvature and its local field value.

In a homogeneous source-free lossless region, a time-harmonic transverse field satisfies ∇²Ẽ + k²Ẽ = 0, with k = ω√(με). The Laplacian describes spatial curvature.

For Eᵧ = A cos(kx + φ), differentiating twice gives d²Eᵧ/dx² = −k²Eᵧ. A positive crest has negative curvature, while a zero crossing has zero second derivative.

If E is measured in V/m, its second spatial derivative is in V/m³. Plotting field and curvature therefore requires separate labeled scales, even when their shapes look similar.

Example

Halving wavelength doubles k = 2π/λ. With unchanged peak field, maximum curvature magnitude becomes four times larger.

    Practice

    1. At a point where Eᵧ = A > 0, what is d²Eᵧ/dx²? Explain the sign using the field's shape.

    Use the sinusoidal crest and the Helmholtz relation.

    The curvature is −k²A. The positive crest bends downward, so the second derivative is negative.
